summary: Describes a revised Microsoft Word template for writing Internet Drafts and RFCs. It replaces the earlier template of RFC 3285, works better with Word's outline modes, and aims to be easier to use. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a ready-made form for a word processor. It helps authors lay out their documents the way the RFC editors expect.

questions: how to write an internet draft in word
subtitle: A Microsoft Word template and post-processing script for writing Internet Drafts and RFCs with what-you-see-is-what-you-get editing.

tldr.problem: Internet Drafts and RFCs were mostly written in compile-based text formatting systems, and an earlier Word template did not support Word's outline-mode renumbering.
tldr.mechanism: A revised Word template (.dot) redefines Word's standard styles, adds RFC-specific ones, and a Perl post-processor cleans up printed text into valid RFC ASCII.
tldr.outcome: Authors can edit in Word and print to a page layout that is line-for-line identical with RFC Editor-compliant ASCII output. It obsoletes RFC 3285.

facts.label: Post-processor limits
facts.value: 66 lines per page, 72 characters per line

today: RFC 5385 is an Informational RFC published through the Independent Submission stream, and it replaces RFC 3285. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Word Template
sections.content:
Internet Drafts and RFCs are predominantly written in embedded-text, compile-based formatting systems. The first is NROFF, driven by embedded commands such as .p for new paragraphs. XML is a more recent alternative that uses structure tags so one file can be compiled into ASCII, HTML and other formats. Neither supports WYSIWYG editing.

This document describes a revised Word template, 2-Word-v2.0.template.dot, meant as an update to the template of RFC 3285. It redefines basic styles rather than creating new ones, updates the boilerplate according to BCP 78, uses more conventional autonumbered references and figures (including name-based references such as [Tou2005]), and supports direct output to a printer as well as the older print-to-text route with post-processing on Windows PCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this, writing an RFC was like typing a recipe in secret code. This template lets you write it in a normal word processor and see the finished page as you go.

sections.title: Using the Template
sections.content:
To use the template, double-click it in Windows so that a new document opens. Do not open it from within Word through File->Open, because that edits the template itself. The RFC says it may work in MacOS or OpenOffice but that is unconfirmed.

Authors should avoid bold, italics, other character formatting, graphics, and paragraph or table borders. It is critical not to use any styles other than those the template provides. New styles include RFC Title, RFC Figure (for ASCII art), RFC List Bullet, RFC List Numbered, RFC References and RFC App. Redefined internal styles such as Normal, Heading1-9, Caption, Header and Footer are used in the normal fashion.

The file can be saved as a Word 97-2003 document or in Word 2007 native format; the RFC says it does not matter which.
sections.plainLanguage: The template comes with its own set of paper-clip labels for titles, lists and figures. You are only supposed to use those labels so everything lines up.

sections.title: Generating Output
sections.content:
The template supports two kinds of output. Printing direct to a printer is line-for-line and page-for-page identical with the text version, apart from minor exceptions: quotes may be angled and hyphens may print as em or en dashes if smart quotes and smart hyphens are enabled.

For a text file, the process has two steps on Windows XP or Vista. First print to the Generic/Text Only printer to produce a .prn file. Then run it through the post-processor in Appendix B. The post-processor omits carriage returns, converts smart quotes and hyphens to ASCII, drops blank lines between page footer and next header and inserts a form feed there, and checks for illegal characters.

There is no support for XML in this template; the RFC says it is being considered for a future revision.
sections.plainLanguage: You can print the page on paper, or turn it into a plain text file with a clean-up helper that fixes curly quotes and page breaks.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3285
sections.content:
The new template borrows heavily from the earlier one. Point sizes, tab locations and the automatic date fields come directly from it. The main changes are:

  • Heading styles: Normal, Heading1-9, Header, Footer and Caption are redefined, because internal style names are needed for outline mode to renumber headings when sections are promoted or demoted.
  • References: autonumbered body paragraphs replace endnotes, because removing the first citation of an endnote reference removed the reference entirely. A second style, RFC References Bookmark, supports name and year tags.
  • Boilerplate: updated to follow BCP 78.
  • Simplification: headers and footers use tabs rather than tables, and smart quotes and hyphens no longer need to be avoided.
  • Direct print and view: print preview matches the compliant ASCII output.

The RFC reports no known compatibility issues; it was designed under Windows XP and Word 2002 and tested under Windows Vista and Word 2007.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version was a rough sketch. This one fixes the parts that were awkward, like references disappearing and headings not renumbering.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that there are many security issues in the general use of Microsoft operating systems and applications. The template is not known to expose any new ones, and it contains no macros as developed and deployed.

The author considered including MD5 signatures of the template and the post-processor. The Perl script is included in the document as an appendix. The template changes to track IETF boilerplate requirements, so its MD5 signature is posted on the author's website for verification instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The template does not run any hidden programs, and the author tells you where to check that your copy has not been tampered with.
